title: Present indicative active: the four conjugations

objectives.can: Give the person and number of a present indicative active and name its conjugation.
Recognise ten of the commonest verbs.

explanation.summary: A Latin verb form says who acts and how many, in one word: *audit*, 'he hears'. This lesson teaches the six personal endings of the present indicative active and the four patterns, called conjugations, by which Latin verbs join those endings to their stems.

sections.heading: Person and number in the ending
body: Latin usually leaves the subject pronoun out, because the ending already says who is acting. In the present indicative active the six endings are: first person singular -o, second -s, third -t; first person plural -mus, second -tis, third -nt. The other tenses change them a little (the imperfect has -m for 'I', for instance), and the perfect has a set of its own, but the idea is the same.

So *habemus* is 'we have' and *habetis* is 'you (plural) have', with no pronoun needed. A pronoun is added for emphasis or contrast: in John 21:17 Peter says *tu scis quia amo te*, and the two pronouns and the two verbs stand side by side. The ending -s always means 'you' in the singular, as in *scis* and *audis*; the ending -tis means 'you' in the plural.

sections.heading: Mood, voice and tense
body: Every finite verb form says four things besides its meaning: person and number (above), tense, voice and mood. The present tense names an action that is going on or is generally true: *credit* may be 'he believes' or 'he is believing', and Latin does not mark the difference. The active voice means that the subject does the action. The indicative mood is the mood of plain statements and questions of fact, which is the mood of almost every main clause in the Gospels.

The other moods (the imperative and the subjunctive) and the passive voice are taught later. In this lesson every verb is present, indicative and active, and the only thing that changes from form to form is the person and number.

sections.heading: The four conjugations
body: Latin verbs fall into four groups by the vowel that joins the stem to the ending. A verb's conjugation is read from its infinitive, the form that dictionaries give after the headword: the first conjugation has -are, the second -ere with a long e, the third -ere with a short e, and the fourth -ire. The editions print no vowel lengths, so you learn which -ere a verb has when you learn the verb.

The first conjugation includes *amo*, *voco* and *laudo*; the second *habeo*, *video*, *moneo* and *timeo*; the third *dico*, *mitto*, *duco* and *credo*; the fourth *audio*, *venio* and *scio*. A group of third-conjugation verbs, such as *facio* and *capio*, take an i before some endings, and are sometimes called 'third-conjugation -io' verbs (some grammars count them as a separate group). They look like the fourth conjugation in *faciunt* and *capiunt*, and like the third elsewhere (*facit*, *facimus*).

The headword of every conjugation is the first person singular of the present: the dictionary lists *amo*, 'I love', and you reach the infinitive and the other forms from it. Because the -o is the same for all four, the second form (the infinitive) is what tells you the conjugation.

sections.heading: How to read a form
body: Work from the end of the word. -mus or -tis shows a plural; -t, -s and -o a singular. Then look at the vowel before the ending: -a- first conjugation, -e- second, -i- third or fourth. The third person plural is the most useful clue between the last two: *dicunt* (third) against *audiunt* (fourth).

In the third conjugation the vowel before -s, -t, -mus and -tis is a short i: *dicis*, *dicit*, *dicimus*, *dicitis*. In the second it is e: *habes*, *habet*, *habemus*, *habetis*. This vowel is the main contrast between the second and third conjugations in the present, and the editions do not print the length of the e, so you must remember the conjugation from the verb, not from the letter.

misunderstandings: The ending -t is not "it", and -nt is not always "they" of persons: both mean the third person, and the subject may be a noun (*Deus dicit*, "God says") or may be left out altogether.
Latin has no separate form for 'I am loving'. *amo* covers both 'I love' and 'I am loving'; the English difference is not marked in the verb.
The Latin ending -o does not show the conjugation, since all four conjugations have -o or -io in the first person. Do not guess the conjugation from the first person alone.
A form in -nt is not necessarily a present tense: imperfects in -bant and futures in -bunt also end in -nt. The tense is read from what comes before the personal ending (the next lesson).

deeper.heading: Principal parts
body: A Latin dictionary lists a verb under its first person singular present. Since the other forms cannot be predicted from it alone, dictionaries add the infinitive, and for many verbs the perfect and a participle as well. These are called the principal parts, and L2.2.1 teaches them. For the regular verbs of this lesson the infinitive is enough to fix the conjugation.

examples.analysis: Three presents, all third person or second person singular. *spirat* (from *spiro*, first conjugation) is third person singular: 'it blows', with *Spiritus* as its subject. *audis* (fourth conjugation, *audio*) is second person singular: 'you hear', and the -s alone says 'you'. *nescis* is the same ending on *nescio*, 'you do not know'. The Latin has no pronoun for 'you' here.

examples.analysis: Two first person plurals, with the ending -mus. *habemus* (second conjugation, *habeo*) is 'we have'; the e before -mus is the mark of the second conjugation. *seducimus* (third conjugation, *seduco*) is 'we lead astray', with the short i before -mus. Both subjects are 'we', and the pronoun *nos* is added only to point at the people themselves.

The subject is the noun *Oves* ('sheep'), which the verb agrees with. *cognosco* is first person singular of the third conjugation: 'I know'. Notice that in both clauses the verb is in the present: Latin states a general truth in the present, as English does.
